summary.text: At Thebes Heracles strangled Hera's serpents in his cradle; after he freed the city from the Minyans, madness drove him to slay Megara's children, and Delphi sent him to serve Eurystheus — first Alcides, then Heracles.

chapters.title: The serpents in the cradle
chapters.text: When Heracles was eight months old, Hera sent two great serpents to destroy him in his bed. The infant rose and strangled them with both hands while Amphitryon and Alcmene looked on — a sign that the elder twin was Zeus' son, though Apollodorus also knows a tale that Amphitryon himself laid the serpents there to learn which boy was his.

chapters.title: Zeus or Amphitryon
chapters.text: Zeus came to Alcmene in Amphitryon's likeness and prolonged the night threefold; she bore Heracles the elder by one night and Iphicles by the mortal husband. Hesiod and Homer name Zeus as sire; the handbook gives both fathers — the archetypal dispute of the hero who is mortal and more than mortal at once.

chapters.title: Megara and the madness
chapters.text: After he overthrew the Minyans of Orchomenus, Creon of Thebes gave him Megara as a prize. Hera drove him mad, and he slew the children he had by her and two sons of Iphicles. Condemned to exile, he went to Delphi — where the Pythia first named him Heracles, though before that he had been called Alcides.

chapters.title: Service at Tiryns
chapters.text: The oracle told him to serve Eurystheus at Tiryns and Mycenae, performing whatever labours the king should set — penance for the slaughter, and Hera's long revenge made into twelve public ordeals that would drive the hero to the ends of the earth.
